title: A Plan to Swap Land Stirs Debate on Cumberland Island
summary:
Wild horses, feral hogs, and deer roam free on Cumberland Island, a Georgia island off the Atlantic coast, 18 miles long. Its salt marshes, forests, and beach can only be reached by ferry. The National Park Service has looked after the island since 1972, including about 9,800 acres of wild land that Congress said should stay in its natural state forever.

But the island is not only wild land. It also has old mission ruins, plantation ruins, and grand homes built long ago by Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy. Their family still lives or spends holidays on land there, and the park service has suggested a land swap that would allow new homes to be built.

Under the plan, park land on the west side would go to two branches of the Carnegie family for up to eight new homes. Park leader Melissa Trenchik says this would help protect nature and historic places on the Atlantic side, where building could then be banned.

Critics say the homes would be far too big, while the family calls the island sacred.
why_it_matters: It matters because the choices grown-ups make about wild places decide whether animals keep a safe home and children can still visit nature in the future.

A salt marsh is a wet, grassy place near the sea where salty water covers the land.
Ruins are the broken parts of old buildings that are left standing.
A plantation is a large farm where crops were grown long ago.
Sacred means very special and holy to a person or a group.

background_read: A national park is a special place that is protected so its wild animals, plants, and old buildings can stay safe.
Some islands can only be reached by boat, which helps keep their wild land quiet and hard to reach.
When people disagree about building on protected land, they sometimes swap one piece of land for another to try to protect the most special parts.
